answer.summary: For a one-sided one-sample t test with 25 participants, detecting a mean increase of 0.2 units with standard deviation 0.5 units at significance level α = 0.05, the statistical power is 0.6173 (approximately 61.73%).
answer.method: Analytical power calculation using the non-central t distribution. Under the alternative hypothesis that the true population mean difference is 0.2 units, the test statistic T = X̄/(s/√n) follows a non-central t distribution with degrees of freedom = 24 and non-centrality parameter λ = (Cohen's d) × √n = 0.4 × 5 = 2.0. Power is computed as P(T > t₀.₀₅,₂₄) = P(T > 1.7109) under this non-central distribution, verified by three independent computational methods (pwr package, direct non-central t integration, and lower-tail probability complement).
assumptions: Outcome is normally distributed with constant variance
One-sided test: null hypothesis H₀: μ = 0 versus alternative H₁: μ > 0 (direction specified a priori)
Standard deviation in population equals 0.5 units
No attrition, missing data, or protocol deviations
Sample size is fixed at n = 25 without intermediate stopping or adaptive modifications
limitations: Power is conditional on the normality assumption; actual power may differ if the outcome is substantially non-normal
Power is sensitive to the true population standard deviation; if SD ≠ 0.5, power will change accordingly
One-sided test has lower power than the equivalent two-sided test; committing to direction a priori is required to achieve this power
Calculation assumes the sample mean and variance are unbiased estimators of the population parameters

# One-sample t test power calculation
# Hypothesis: one-sided test (upper tail)
# H0: mu = 0
# H1: mu > 0
# Effect to detect: 0.2 units
# Standard deviation: 0.5 units
# Sample size: 25 participants
# Significance level: 0.05, one-sided

# Parameters
n <- 25
effect_size_raw <- 0.2  # mean difference in original units
sd <- 0.5
alpha <- 0.05
df <- n - 1  # degrees of freedom for one-sample t test

# Standardized effect size (Cohen's d)
cohens_d <- effect_size_raw / sd

# Non-centrality parameter for t distribution
ncp <- cohens_d * sqrt(n)

# Critical t-value for one-sided test at alpha 0.05
t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)

# Power: P(T > t_crit | H1 is true)
# Under H1, the test statistic follows non-central t distribution
power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp)

# Verification using pwr package
library(pwr)
power_pwr <- pwr.t.test(n = n, d = cohens_d, sig.level = alpha, 
                         alternative = "greater", type = "one.sample")$power

cat("One-sample t test power calculation\n")
cat("=====================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Sample size (n): %d\n", n))
cat(sprintf("Mean difference (effect): %.1f units\n", effect_size_raw))
cat(sprintf("Standard deviation: %.1f units\n", sd))
cat(sprintf("Cohen's d: %.2f\n", cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("Non-centrality parameter: %.4f\n", ncp))
cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom: %d\n", df))
cat(sprintf("Critical t-value (alpha=0.05, one-sided): %.4f\n", t_crit))
cat(sprintf("\nPower (using non-central t distribution): %.6f\n", power))
cat(sprintf("Power (using pwr package): %.6f\n", power_pwr))

# Format for output
results_df <- data.frame(
  metric = "power",
  value = power,
  unit = "probability"
)

cat("\n=====================================\n")
print(results_df)

# Export for POWER_AGENT_RESULT
